title: IoT Malware Uses Public Linux Exploits to Gain Root and Turn Devices Into DDoS Bots
content_md: A newly identified IoT malware family named KATARU is targeting Linux-based devices through Telnet credential brute-force attacks, then attempting to gain root access and enlist compromised systems into a DDoS botnet. The malware was observed after attackers brute-forced Telnet credentials on a honeypot from the IP address 160[.]191.242.92 . Following successful access, the attacker used BusyBox commands to download and run an ARM payload named vlxx.arm . KATARU shares several features with Mirai-style botnets, including DDoS attack functions and brute-force capabilities. However, researchers found that it also includes a broad set of Linux privilege-escalation exploits, persistence methods, encrypted command-and-control communications, anti-analysis checks, and decoy network traffic. Linux Exploits Create Botnets After execution, KATARU first checks whether /etc/passwd is writable. If it is, the malware attempts to remove the root password placeholder, allowing the attacker to run su and gain root privileges without entering a password. If that method fails, the malware tries several public Linux local privilege-escalation exploits, including code for CVE-2026-46300, known as Fragnesia; CVE-2026-43284, called DirtyFrag; and CVE-2026-31431, known as Copy Fail. Decompilation of exploit code found in the sample (Source: nozominetworks) The sample also attempts a cgroup v1 release_agent escape.
